expect: Describe the Jewish mourning rituals of shiva, avelut and yahrzeit.
value: Explain two ways in which Jewish mourning rituals support a family after a death.
note: F24: a 3-mark Describe part does not exist on this paper. This lesson already has two outline-three questions, so this becomes the (b) explain-two form.

expect: 3 marks — Describe
value: 4 marks — Explain Two
note: F24: matches the (b) form.

expect: One mark each. Shiva: seven-day mourning period in which the immediate family stays at home receiving visitors and community support. Avelut: the extended 30-day period (and first year) of gradually returning to normal life while continuing mourning practices. Yahrzeit: the annual anniversary of death, marked by lighting a memorial candle and reciting the Kaddish prayer.
value: 2 marks per way. Way 1: shiva keeps the immediate family at home for seven days while the community visits and brings food, so mourners are never left alone and are freed from ordinary duties at the hardest moment. Way 2: avelut sets a staged return to normal life over 30 days, and the first year for a parent, and yahrzeit brings the family back every year to light a memorial candle and recite Kaddish — grief is given a lasting place instead of being rushed.
note: F24: mark scheme rewritten for the explain-two form.

expect: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Shabbat is commanded in the Decalogue (Exodus 20) — one of the Ten Commandments; Exodus 31:12-18 calls it the sign of the covenant for all generations; it is observed every week, giving it greater frequency than any festival; Rabbi Heschel called Shabbat a 'cathedral in time'; the Talmud treats Shabbat observance as a test case for overall Torah commitment. Arguments against: Yom Kippur is described as the holiest day of the year — its intense focus on atonement and the forgiveness of sins is theologically profound; Pesach commemorates the foundational event of Jewish history (the Exodus); the Shema and Amidah (recited daily) may have a stronger claim on daily Jewish identity than weekly Shabbat; different Jewish communities emphasise different practices. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Exodus 31:12-18 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.
